content: Proven diagnostic tests should be utilized to ensure accurate detection and management of CMV (cytomegalovirus) infections. Recipients and candidates for hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) must avoid sharing cups, glasses, and eating utensils with others, including family members, to minimize the risk of CMV exposure. This recommendation is supported by evidence (BIII). Sexually active individuals who are not in long-term monogamous relationships should consistently use latex condoms during sexual activity to reduce the risk of CMV exposure and other sexually transmitted infections. This is a strong recommendation based on evidence (AII). Even in long-term monogamous relationships, partners may have discordant CMV infection statuses. Therefore, during periods of immunosuppression, sexually active HSCT recipients in monogamous relationships should request their partners to undergo serum CMV IgG antibody testing. If the couple is discordant, the use of latex condoms during sexual contact is advised to reduce the risk of CMV transmission (CIII). HSCT candidates and recipients should practice regular handwashing after handling or changing diapers or after wiping oral and nasal secretions to reduce the risk of CMV exposure. This is a strong recommendation based on evidence (AII). HSCT recipients who are CMV-seronegative (R-negative or D-negative) should only receive leukocyte-reduced or CMV-seronegative red blood cells or leukocyte-reduced platelets (containing fewer than 1 x 10^6 leukocytes per unit) to prevent transfusion-associated CMV infection (AI). Healthcare workers (HCWs) must wear gloves when handling blood products or other potentially contaminated biological materials to prevent CMV transmission to HSCT recipients. This is a strong recommendation based on evidence (AII). HSCT patients known to excrete CMV should be placed under standard precautions for the duration of CMV excretion to prevent possible transmission to CMV-seronegative HSCT recipients and candidates (AIII). Physicians should be aware that CMV excretion can be episodic or prolonged. Physicians should use either prophylaxis or preemptive treatment with ganciclovir for allogeneic HSCT recipients (AI). When selecting a CMV disease prevention strategy, physicians should carefully evaluate the risks and benefits of each approach, the specific needs and condition of the patient, and the virology laboratory support capabilities of the hospital. The induction course of treatment is typically initiated at the time of engraftment (AI), although a brief prophylactic course may be added during HSCT preconditioning (CIII). For CMV-seropositive donors (D-positive) or recipients (R-negative), the risk of active CMV infection is low if screened or filtered blood product support is used (BII). The preemptive strategy involves restricting ganciclovir use to patients who show evidence of CMV infection after HSCT. This approach requires the use of sensitive and specific laboratory tests to rapidly diagnose CMV infection and enable immediate administration of ganciclovir upon detection of CMV infection. Physicians should select one of two diagnostic tests to determine the need for preemptive treatment. Currently, the detection of CMV pp65 antigen in leukocytes (antigenemia) is preferred for screening for preemptive treatment because it is faster and more sensitive than culture methods and has a good positive predictive value. Direct detection of CMV DNA using polymerase chain reaction (PCR) is highly sensitive but has a lower positive predictive value. Plasma CMV DNA PCR is particularly useful during neutropenia when the leukocyte count is too low for CMV pp65 antigenemia testing. Virus culture of urine, saliva, blood, or bronchoalveolar washings using rapid shell-vial culture or routine culture methods can be employed. However, viral culture techniques are less sensitive than CMV DNA PCR or CMV pp65 antigenemia tests. Rapid shell-vial cultures require at least 48 hours, and routine viral cultures may take weeks to yield final results. Consequently, viral culture techniques are less satisfactory compared to PCR or antigenemia tests.
